gap: No result ChatGPT got says that every power bank that skips airline approval stops at about 99.5 Wh, so 'biggest' is a tie and the real differences are cost per Wh ($1.20/Wh for the AOHi Future Starship at $119 vs $1.77/Wh for the EcoFlow RAPID Pro at $175.99) and how much reaches a laptop (about 81 of the RAPID Pro's 99.54 Wh in Macworld's MacBook Pro 14 test, roughly 82%).
standout_why: All 17 results ChatGPT got are rule pages: FAA PackSafe pages and posters, the IATA power-bank guidance PDF, 49 CFR 175.10 on govinfo, Cornell LII and faraim, and American Airlines restricted-items pages. None names a product, weight, price or delivered energy. Caveat: I could not read their full text. FAA and aa.com returned HTTP 403, and the IATA PDF came back as binary with only its metadata readable (dated 2026-03-31). So the claim that they hold no product numbers rests on their titles and the kind of page they are, plus ChatGPT's answer, which quotes only Wh limits and mAh conversions.
decides: This confirms the page's angle: pick a bank of about 99 Wh. Capacity is capped at the same level for every candidate, so the pick comes down to price and weight per Wh. The AOHi Future Starship 240W gives the most Wh per dollar at $1.20/Wh. The EcoFlow RAPID Pro costs about 47% more per Wh ($1.77) and weighs 1.54 lb. Anker's current Prime 26K 300W is the lightest bank I could source (1.32 lb), but anker.com US only listed it bundled with a charging base at $329.99. Our page's Anker row points to a URL (a1340) that returned 404 today. Going over 100 Wh (the AOHi Starship 40K, $179) needs airline approval for a bank ChatGPT's answer says some airlines now cap at 100 Wh, so it should stay a footnote.
